entries.181dabbc56e123abb05d52474747a567b55a9996: <div sID="gen34158" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="14" osisID="Rev.14" sID="Rev.14"/> <div eID="gen34158" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34159" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen34160" type="x-p"/> After an account of the great trials and sufferings which the servants of God had endured, we have now a more pleasant scene opening; the day begins now to dawn, and here we have represented, I. The Lord Jesus at the head of his faithful followers, <reference osisRef="Rev.14.1-Rev.14.5">ver. 1-5</reference>. II. Three angels sent successively to proclaim the fall of Babylon and the things antecedent and consequent to so great an event, <reference osisRef="Rev.14.6-Rev.14.13">ver. 6-13</reference>. III. The vision of the harvest, <reference osisRef="Rev.14.14-Rev.14.20">ver. 14</reference>, &c.
entries.9a50c15525f9d37149fb66bc58b25f72a00dc9af: <div eID="gen34160" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen34159" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">The Lamb and His Attendants. (<hi type="small-caps">a. d.</hi> 95.)</title> <div sID="gen34161" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> And I looked, and, lo, a Lamb stood on the mount Sion, and with him a hundred forty <hi type="italic">and</hi> four thousand, having his Father's name written in their foreheads. <hi type="super">2</hi> And I heard a voice from heaven, as the voice of many waters, and as the voice of a great thunder: and I heard the voice of harpers harping with their harps: <hi type="super">3</hi> And they sung as it were a new song before the throne, and before the four beasts, and the elders: and no man could learn that song but the hundred <hi type="italic">and</hi> forty <hi type="italic">and</hi> four thousand, which were redeemed from the earth. 4 These are they which were not defiled with women; for they are virgins. These are they which follow the Lamb whithersoever he goeth. These were redeemed from among men, <hi type="italic">being</hi> the firstfruits unto God and to the Lamb. <hi type="super">5</hi> And in their mouth was found no guile: for they are without fault before the throne of God. <div eID="gen34161" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34162" type="x-p"/> Here we have one of the most pleasing sights that can be viewed in this world—the Lord Jesus Christ at the head of his faithful adherents and attendants. Here observe, 1. How Christ appears: as a Lamb standing upon <hi type="italic">mount Zion.</hi> Mount Zion is the gospel church. Christ is with his church and in the midst of her in all her troubles, and therefore she is not consumed. It is his presence that secures her perseverance; he appears as <hi type="italic">a Lamb, a true Lamb, the Lamb of God.</hi> A counterfeit lamb is mentioned as rising out of the earth in the last chapter, which was really a dragon; here Christ appears as the true paschal Lamb, to show that his mediatorial government is the fruit of his sufferings, and the cause of his people's safety and fidelity. 2. How his people appear: very honourably. (1.) As to the numbers, they are many, even all who are sealed; not one of them lost in all the tribulations through which they have gone. (2.) Their distinguishing badge: they had <hi type="italic">the name of God written in their foreheads;</hi> they made a bold and open profession of their faith in God and Christ, and, this being followed by suitable actings, they are known and approved. (3.) Their congratulations and songs of praise, which were peculiar to the redeemed (<reference osisRef="Rev.14.3">v. 3</reference>); their praises were loud as thunder, or <hi type="italic">as the voice of many waters;</hi> they were melodious, as <hi type="italic">of harpers;</hi> they were heavenly, <hi type="italic">before the throne</hi> of God. <hi type="italic">The song was new,</hi> suited to the new covenant, and unto that new and gracious dispensation of Providence under which they now were; and their song was a secret to others, <hi type="italic">strangers intermeddled not with their joy;</hi> others might repeat the words of the song, but they were strangers to the true sense and spirit of it. (4.) Their character and description. [1.] They are described by their chastity and purity: <hi type="italic">They are virgins.</hi> They had not defiled themselves either with corporal or spiritual adultery; they had kept themselves clean from the abominations of the antichristian generation. [2.] By their loyalty and stedfast adherence to Christ: <hi type="italic">They follow the Lamb withersoever he goes;</hi> they follow the conduct of his word, Spirit, and providence, leaving it to him to lead them into what duties and difficulties he pleases. [3.] By their former designation to this honour: <hi type="italic">These were redeemed from among men, being the first-fruits to God, and to the Lamb,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rev.14.4">v. 4</reference>. Here is plain evidence of a special redemption: <hi type="italic">They were redeemed from among men.</hi> Some of the children of men are, by redeeming mercy, distinguished from others: <hi type="italic">They were the first-fruits to God, and to the Lamb,</hi> his choice ones, eminent in every grace, and the earnest of many more who should <hi type="italic">be followers of them, as they were of Christ.</hi> [4.] By their universal integrity and conscientiousness: <hi type="italic">There was no guile found in them,</hi> and <hi type="italic">they were without fault before the throne of God.</hi> They were without any prevailing guile, any allowed fault; their hearts were right with God, and, as for their human infirmities, they were freely pardoned in Christ. This is the happy remnant who attend upon the Lord Jesus as their head and Lord; he is glorified in them, and they are glorified in him.
entries.4e0a681677fcc7821c7b78c7d7bd39cec5b78cf7: <div eID="gen34162" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Three Angels. (<hi type="small-caps">a. d.</hi> 95.)</title> <div sID="gen34163" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">6</hi> And I saw another angel fly in the midst of heaven, having the everlasting gospel to preach unto them that dwell on the earth, and to every nation, and kindred, and tongue, and people, <hi type="super">7</hi> Saying with a loud voice, Fear God, and give glory to him; for the hour of his judgment is come: and worship him that made heaven, and earth, and the sea, and the fountains of waters. <hi type="super">8</hi> And there followed another angel, saying, Babylon is fallen, is fallen, that great city, because she made all nations drink of the wine of the wrath of her fornication. <hi type="super">9</hi> And the third angel followed them, saying with a loud voice, If any man worship the beast and his image, and receive <hi type="italic">his</hi> mark in his forehead, or in his hand, <hi type="super">10</hi> The same shall drink of the wine of the wrath of God, which is poured out without mixture into the cup of his indignation; and he shall be tormented with fire and brimstone in the presence of the holy angels, and in the presence of the Lamb: <hi type="super">11</hi> And the smoke of their torment ascendeth up for ever and ever: and they have no rest day nor night, who worship the beast and his image, and whosoever receiveth the mark of his name. <hi type="super">12</hi> Here is the patience of the saints: here <hi type="italic">are</hi> they that keep the commandments of God, and the faith of Jesus. <div eID="gen34163" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34164" type="x-p"/> In this part of the chapter we have three angels or messengers sent from heaven to give notice of the fall of Babylon, and of those things that were antecedent and consequent to that great event. <div eID="gen34164" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34165" type="x-p"/> I. The first angel was sent on an errand antecedent to it, and that was <hi type="italic">to preach the everlasting gospel,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rev.14.6-Rev.14.7">v. 6, 7</reference>. Observe, 1. The gospel is an everlasting gospel; it is so in its nature, and it will be so in its consequences. Though all flesh be grass, the word of the Lord endureth for ever. 2. It is a work fit for an angel to preach this everlasting gospel; such is the dignity, and such is the difficulty of that work! And yet we have this treasure in earthen vessels. 3. The everlasting gospel is of great concern to all the world; and, as it is the concern of all, it is very much to be desired that it should be made known to all, even <hi type="italic">to every nation, and kindred, and tongue, and people.</hi> 4. The gospel is the great means whereby men are brought to fear God, and to give glory to him. Natural religion is not sufficient to keep up the fear of God, nor to secure to him glory from men; it is the gospel that revives the fear of God, and retrieves his glory in the world. 5. When idolatry creeps into the churches of God, it is by the preaching of the gospel, attended by the power of the Holy Spirit, that men are <hi type="italic">turned from idols to serve the living God,</hi> as the Creator of <hi type="italic">the heaven, and the earth, and the sea, and the fountains of waters,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rev.14.7">v. 7</reference>. To worship any God besides him who created the world is idolatry. <div eID="gen34165" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34166" type="x-p"/> II. The second angel follows the other, and proclaims the actual fall of Babylon. The preaching of the everlasting gospel had shaken the foundations of antichristianism in the world, and hastened its downfall. By Babylon is generally understood Rome, which was before called <hi type="italic">Sodom</hi> and <hi type="italic">Egypt,</hi> for wickedness and cruelty, and is now first called <hi type="italic">Babylon,</hi> for pride and idolatry. Observe, 1. What God has fore-ordained and foretold shall be done as certainly as if it were done already. 2. The greatness of the papal Babylon will not be able to prevent her fall, but will make it more dreadful and remarkable. 3. The wickedness of Babylon, in corrupting, debauching, and intoxicating the nations round about her, will make her fall just and will declare the righteousness of God in her utter ruin, <reference osisRef="Rev.14.8">v. 8</reference>. Her crimes are recited as the just cause of her destruction. <div eID="gen34166" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34167" type="x-p"/> III. A third angel follows the other two, and gives warning to all of that divine vengeance which would overtake all those that obstinately adhered to the antichristian interest after God had thus proclaimed its downfall, <reference osisRef="Rev.14.9-Rev.14.10">v. 9, 10</reference>. If after this (this threatening denounced against Babylon, and in part already executed) any should persist in their idolatry, professing subjection to the beast and promoting his cause, they must expect <hi type="italic">to drink deep of the wind of the wrath of God;</hi> they shall be forever miserable in soul and body; Jesus Christ will inflict this punishment upon them, and the holy angels will behold it and approve of it. Idolatry, both pagan and papal, is a damning sin in its own nature, and will prove fatal to those who persist in it, after fair warning given by the word of Providence; those who refuse to come out of Babylon, when thus called, and resolve to partake of her sins, must receive of her plagues; and the guilt and ruin of such incorrigible idolaters will serve to set forth the excellency of the patience and obedience of the saints. These graces shall be rewarded with salvation and glory. When the treachery and rebellion of others shall be punished with everlasting destruction, then it will be said, to the honour of the faithful (<reference osisRef="Rev.14.12">v. 12</reference>): <hi type="italic">Here is the patience of the saints;</hi> you have before seen their patience exercised, now you see it rewarded.
entries.06f6f1704aa2ef43f4ca4d2128a5041ab3af4fb3: <div eID="gen34167" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Harvest and the Vintage. (<hi type="small-caps">a. d.</hi> 95.)</title> <div sID="gen34168" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">13</hi> And I heard a voice from heaven saying unto me, Write, Blessed <hi type="italic">are</hi> the dead which die in the Lord from henceforth: Yea, saith the Spirit, that they may rest from their labours; and their works do follow them. <hi type="super">14</hi> And I looked, and behold a white cloud, and upon the cloud <hi type="italic">one</hi> sat like unto the Son of man, having on his head a golden crown, and in his hand a sharp sickle. <hi type="super">15</hi> And another angel came out of the temple, crying with a loud voice to him that sat on the cloud, Thrust in thy sickle, and reap: for the time is come for thee to reap; for the harvest of the earth is ripe. <hi type="super">16</hi> And he that sat on the cloud thrust in his sickle on the earth; and the earth was reaped. <hi type="super">17</hi> And another angel came out of the temple which is in heaven, he also having a sharp sickle. <hi type="super">18</hi> And another angel came out from the altar, which had power over fire; and cried with a loud cry to him that had the sharp sickle, saying, Thrust in thy sharp sickle, and gather the clusters of the vine of the earth; for her grapes are fully ripe. <hi type="super">19</hi> And the angel thrust in his sickle into the earth, and gathered the vine of the earth, and cast <hi type="italic">it</hi> into the great winepress of the wrath of God. <hi type="super">20</hi> And the winepress was trodden without the city, and blood came out of the winepress, even unto the horse bridles, by the space of a thousand <hi type="italic">and</hi> six hundred furlongs. <div eID="gen34168" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34169" type="x-p"/> Here we have the vision of the harvest and vintage, introduced with a solemn preface. Observe, <div eID="gen34169" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34170" type="x-p"/> I. The preface, <reference osisRef="Rev.14.13">v. 13</reference>. Here note, 1. Whence this prophecy about the harvest came: it came down from heaven, and not from men, and therefore it is of certain truth and great authority. 2. How it was to be preserved and published—by writing; it was to be a matter of record, that the people of God might have recourse to it for their support and comfort upon all occasions. 3. What it principally intended, and that is, to show the blessedness of all the faithful saints and servants of God, both in death and after death: <hi type="italic">Blessed are the dead that die in the Lord from henceforth,</hi> &c. Here observe, (1.) The description of those that are and shall be blessed—such as die in the Lord, either die in the cause of Christ, or rather die in a state of vital union with Christ, such as are found in Christ when death comes. (2.) The demonstration of this blessedness: <hi type="italic">They rest from their labours, and their works do follow them.</hi> [1.] They are blessed in their rest; they rest from all sin, temptation, sorrow, and persecution. <hi type="italic">There the wicked cease from troubling, there the weary are at rest.</hi> [2.] They are blessed in their recompence: <hi type="italic">Their works follow them;</hi> they do not go before them as their title, or price of purchase, but follow them as their evidence of having lived and died in the Lord; and the memory of them will be pleasant, and the reward glorious, far above the merit of all their services and sufferings. [3.] They are happy in the time of their dying, when they have lived to see the cause of God reviving, the peace of the church returning, and the wrath of God falling upon their idolatrous cruel enemies. Such times are good times to die in; they have Simeon's desire: <hi type="italic">Now, Lord, let thou thy servant depart in peace, for mine eyes have seen thy salvation.</hi> And all this is ratified and confirmed by the testimony of the Spirit witnessing with their spirits and with the written word. <div eID="gen34170" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34171" type="x-p"/> II. We have the vision itself, represented by a harvest and a vintage. <div eID="gen34171" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34172" type="x-p"/> 1. By a harvest (<reference osisRef="Rev.14.14-Rev.14.15">v. 14, 15</reference>), an emblem that sometimes signifies the cutting down of the wicked, when ripe for ruin, by the judgments of God, and sometimes the gathering in of the righteous, when ripe for heaven, by the mercy of God. This seems rather to represent God's judgments against the wicked: and here observe, <div eID="gen34172" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34173" type="x-p"/> (1.) The Lord of the harvest—one so <hi type="italic">like unto the Son of man</hi> that he was the same, even the Lord Jesus, who is described, [1.] By the chariot in which he sat—<hi type="italic">a white cloud,</hi> a cloud that had a bright side turned to the church, how dark soever it might be to the wicked. [2.] By the ensign of his power: <hi type="italic">On his head was a golden crown,</hi> authority to do all that he did and whatsoever he would do. [3.] By the instrument of his providences: <hi type="italic">In his hand a sharp sickle.</hi> [4.] By the solicitations he had from the temple to perform this great work. What he did, he was desired to do by his people; and, though he was resolved to do it, he would for this thing be sought unto by them, and so it should be in return to their prayers. <div eID="gen34173" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34174" type="x-p"/> (2.) The harvest-work, which is, to thrust the sickle into the corn, and reap the field. The sickle is the sword of God's justice; the field is the world; reaping is cutting the inhabitants of the earth down and carrying them off. <div eID="gen34174" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34175" type="x-p"/> (3.) The harvest-time; and this is when the corn is ripe, when the measure of the sin of men is filled up, and they are ripe for destruction. The most inveterate enemies of Christ and his church are not destroyed till by their sin they are ripe for ruin, and then he will spare them no longer; he will thrust in his sickle, and the earth shall be reaped. <div eID="gen34175" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34176" type="x-p"/> 2. By a vintage, <reference osisRef="Rev.14.17">v. 17</reference>. Some think that these two are only different emblems of the same judgment; others that they refer to distinct events of providence before the end of all things. Observe, (1.) To whom this vintage-work was committed—to an angel, <hi type="italic">another angel that came out from the altar,</hi> that is, from the holiest of all in heaven. (2.) At whose request this vintage-work was undertaken: it was, as before, at the cry of an <hi type="italic">angel out of the temple,</hi> the ministers and churches of God on earth. (3.) The work of the vintage, which consists of two parts:—[1.] The cutting off, and <hi type="italic">gathering, the clusters of the vine,</hi> which were now ripe and ready, <hi type="italic">fully ripe,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rev.14.18">v. 18</reference>. [2.] Casting these grapes <hi type="italic">into the wine-press</hi> (<reference osisRef="Rev.14.19">v. 19</reference>); here we are told, <hi type="italic">First,</hi> What was the wine-press: it was <hi type="italic">the wrath of God,</hi> the fire of his indignation, some terrible calamity, very probably the sword, shedding the blood of the wicked. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> Where was the place of the wine-press—<hi type="italic">without the city,</hi> where the army lay that came against Babylon. <hi type="italic">Thirdly,</hi> The quantity of the wine, that is, of the blood that was drawn forth by this judgment: it was, for depth, up <hi type="italic">to the horses' bridles,</hi> and, for breadth and length, <hi type="italic">a thousand and six hundred furlongs</hi> (<reference osisRef="Rev.14.20">v. 20</reference>); that is, say some, 200 Italian miles, which is thought to be the measure of the holy land, and may be meant of the patrimony of the holy see, encompassing the city of Rome. But here we are left of doubtful conjectures. Perhaps this great event has not yet had its accomplishment, but <hi type="italic">the vision is for an appointed time;</hi> and therefore, though it may seem to tarry, we are to wait for it. <hi type="italic">But who shall live when the Lord does this?</hi>  <chapter eID="Rev.14"/> <div eID="gen34176" type="x-p"/>

entries.511eec5421e99a1e4d3c8d6e1e46bbcae4cfacbd: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv19267"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 14</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Rev.14.1-Rev.14.20">Re 14:1-20</reference>. The Lamb Seen on Zion with the 144,000. Their Song. The Gospel Proclaimed before the End by One Angel: The Fall of Babylon, by Another: The Doom of the Beast Worshippers, by a Third. The Blessedness of the Dead in the Lord. The Harvest. The Vintage.</title> <div sID="gen42025" type="x-p"/> In contrast to the beast, false prophet, and apostate Church (<reference osisRef="Rev.13.1-Rev.13.18">Re 13:1-18</reference>) and introductory to the announcement of judgments about to descend on them and the world (<reference osisRef="Rev.14.8-Rev.14.11">Re 14:8-11</reference>, anticipatory of <reference osisRef="Rev.18.2-Rev.18.6">Re 18:2-6</reference>), stand here the redeemed, "the divine kernel of humanity, the positive fruits of the history of the world and the Church" [Auberlen]. The fourteenth through sixteenth chapters describe the preparations for the Messianic judgment. As the fourteenth chapter begins with the 144,000 of Israel (compare <reference osisRef="Rev.7.4-Rev.7.8">Re 7:4-8</reference>, no longer exposed to trial as then, but now triumphant), so the fifteenth chapter begins with those who have overcome from among the Gentiles (compare <reference osisRef="Rev.15.1-Rev.15.5">Re 15:1-5</reference> with <reference osisRef="Rev.7.9-Rev.7.17">Re 7:9-17</reference>); the two classes of elect forming together the whole company of transfigured saints who shall reign with Christ.<div eID="gen42025" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42026" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv19267"/><hi type="bold">1. a--</hi>A, B, C, Coptic, and Origen read, "the."<div eID="gen42026" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42027" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Lamb ... on ... Sion--</hi>having left His position "in the midst of the throne," and now taking His stand on Sion.<div eID="gen42027" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42028" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">his Father's name--</hi>A, B, and C read, "His name and His Father's name."<div eID="gen42028" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42029" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">in--</hi>Greek, "upon." God's and Christ's name here answers to the seal "upon their foreheads" in <reference osisRef="Rev.7.3">Re 7:3</reference>. As the 144,000 of Israel are "the first-fruits" (<reference osisRef="Rev.14.4">Re 14:4</reference>), so "the harvest" (<reference osisRef="Rev.14.15">Re 14:15</reference>) is the general assembly of Gentile saints to be translated by Christ as His first act in assuming His kingdom, prior to His judgment (<reference osisRef="Rev.16.17-Rev.16.21">Re 16:17-21</reference>, the last seven vials) on the Antichristian world, in executing which His saints shall share. As Noah and Lot were taken seasonably out of the judgment, but exposed to the trial to the last moment [De Burgh], so those who shall reign with Christ shall first suffer with Him, being delivered out of the judgments, but not out of the trials. The Jews are meant by "the saints of the Most High": against them Antichrist makes war, changing their times and laws; for true Israelites cannot join in the idolatry of the beast, any more than true Christians. The common affliction will draw closely together, in opposing the beast's worship, the Old Testament and New Testament people of God. Thus the way is paved for Israel's conversion. This last utter scattering of the holy people's power leads them, under the Spirit, to seek Messiah, and to cry at His approach, "Blessed is He that cometh in the name of the Lord." <div eID="gen42029" type="x-p"/>
entries.1f980ba341d8eec8f5ebe1d79bb2f2aa69511b32: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv19268"/><div sID="gen42030" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv19268"/><hi type="bold">2. from--</hi>Greek, "out of."<div eID="gen42030" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42031" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">voice of many waters--</hi>as is the voice of Himself, such also is the voice of His people.<div eID="gen42031" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42032" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">I heard the voice of harpers--</hi>A, B, C, and Origen read, "the voice which I heard (was) as of harpers." <div eID="gen42032" type="x-p"/>
entries.f366540e969a10d343dc7a7c3a754766335266c0: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv19269"/><div sID="gen42033" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv19269"/><hi type="bold">3. sung--</hi>Greek, "sing."<div eID="gen42033" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42034" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">as it were--</hi>So A, C, and Vulgate read. It is "as it were" a new song; for it is, in truth, as old as God's eternal purpose. But B, Syriac, Coptic, Origen, and Andreas omit these words.<div eID="gen42034" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42035" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">new song--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Rev.5.9">Re 5:9</reference>, <reference osisRef="Rev.5.10">10</reference>). The song is that of victory after conflict with the dragon, beast, and false prophet: never sung before, for such a conflict had never been fought before; therefore new: till now the kingdom of Christ on earth had been usurped; they sing the new song in anticipation of His blood-bought kingdom with His saints.<div eID="gen42035" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42036" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">four beasts--</hi>rather, as Greek, "four living creatures." The harpers and singers evidently include the 144,000: so the parallel proves (<reference osisRef="Rev.15.2">Re 15:2</reference>, <reference osisRef="Rev.15.3">3</reference>), where the same act is attributed to the general company of the saints, the harvest (<reference osisRef="Rev.14.15">Re 14:15</reference>) from all nations. Not as Alford, "the harpers and song are in heaven, but the 144,000 are on earth."<div eID="gen42036" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42037" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">redeemed--</hi>literally, "purchased." Not even the angels can learn that song, for they know not experimentally what it is to have "come out of the great tribulation, and washed their robes white in the blood of the Lamb" (<reference osisRef="Rev.7.14">Re 7:14</reference>). <div eID="gen42037" type="x-p"/>
entries.505cd62d08be7c72332abbc8df4943331624026c: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv19270"/><div sID="gen42038" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv19270"/><hi type="bold">4. virgins--</hi>spiritually (<reference osisRef="Matt.25.1">Mt 25:1</reference>); in contrast to the apostate Church, Babylon (<reference osisRef="Rev.14.8">Re 14:8</reference>), spiritually "a harlot" (<reference osisRef="Rev.17.1-Rev.17.5">Re 17:1-5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.1.21">Is 1:21</reference>; contrast <reference osisRef="2Cor.11.2">2Co 11:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Eph.5.25-Eph.5.27">Ep 5:25-27</reference>). Their not being defiled with women means they were not led astray from Christian faithfulness by the tempters who jointly constitute the spiritual "harlot."<div eID="gen42038" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42039" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">follow the Lamb whithersoever he goeth--</hi>in glory, being especially near His person; the fitting reward of their following Him so fully on earth.<div eID="gen42039" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42040" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">redeemed--</hi>"purchased."<div eID="gen42040" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42041" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">being the--</hi>rather, "as a first-fruit." Not merely a "first-fruit" in the sense in which all believers are so, but Israel's 144,000 elect are the first-fruit, the Jewish and Gentile elect Church is the harvest; in a further sense, the whole of the transfigured and translated Church which reigns with Christ at His coming, is the first-fruit, and the consequent general ingathering of Israel and the nations, ending in the last judgment, is the full and final harvest. <div eID="gen42041" type="x-p"/>
entries.c72019131e0432e197d5c697effbc1280dcc0b93: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv19271"/><div sID="gen42042" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv19271"/><hi type="bold">5. guile--</hi>So Andreas in one copy. But A, B, C, Origen, and Andreas in other copies read, "falsehood." Compare with English Version reading <reference osisRef="Ps.32.2">Psa 32:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.53.9">Is 53:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="John.1.47">Joh 1:47</reference>.<div eID="gen42042" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42043" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">for--</hi>So B, Syriac, Coptic, Origen, and Andreas read. But A and C omit.<div eID="gen42043" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42044" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">without fault--</hi>Greek, "blameless": in respect to the sincerity of their fidelity to Him. Not absolutely, and in themselves blameless; but regarded as such on the ground of His righteousness in whom alone they trusted, and whom they faithfully served by His Spirit in them. The allusion seems to be to <reference osisRef="Ps.15.1">Psa 15:1</reference>, 2. Compare <reference osisRef="Rev.14.1">Re 14:1</reference>, "stood on Mount Sion."<div eID="gen42044" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42045" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">before the throne of God--</hi>A, B, C, Syriac, Coptic, Origen, and Andreas omit these words. The oldest Vulgate manuscript supports them. <div eID="gen42045" type="x-p"/>
entries.8fe28bcc6e391528a52883031812c15037fcca7e: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv19272"/><div sID="gen42046" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv19272"/>6. Here begins the portion relating to the Gentile world, as the former portion related to Israel. Before the end the Gospel is to be preached for a WITNESS unto all nations: not that all nations shall be converted, but all nations shall have had the opportunity given them of deciding whether they will be for, or against, Christ. Those thus preached to are "they that dwell (so A, Coptic, and Syriac read. But B, C, Origen, Vulgate, Cyprian, 312, read, 'SIT,' compare <reference osisRef="Matt.4.16">Mt 4:16</reference>; <reference osisRef="Luke.1.79">Lu 1:79</reference>, having their settled home) on the earth," being of earth earthy: this last season of grace is given them, if yet they may repent, before "judgment" (<reference osisRef="Rev.14.7">Re 14:7</reference>) descends: if not, they will be left without excuse, as the world which resisted the preaching of Noah in the the hundred twenty years "while the long-suffering of God waited." "So also the prophets gave the people a last opportunity of repentance before the Babylonian destruction of Jerusalem, and our Lord and His apostles before the Roman destruction of the holy city" [Auberlen]. The Greek for "unto" (epi, in A and C) means literally, "upon," or "over," or "in respect to" (<reference osisRef="Mark.9.12">Mr 9:12</reference>; <reference osisRef="Heb.7.13">He 7:13</reference>). So also "TO every nation" (Greek, "epi," in A, B, C, Vulgate, Syriac, Origen, Andreas, Cyprian, and Primasius). This, perhaps, implies that the Gospel, though diffused over the globe, shall not come savingly unto any save the elect. The world is not to be evangelized till Christ shall come: meanwhile, God's purpose is "to take out of the Gentiles a people for His name," to be witnesses of the effectual working of His Spirit during the counter-working of "the mystery of iniquity."<div eID="gen42046" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42047" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">everlasting gospel--</hi>the Gospel which announces the glad tidings of the everlasting kingdom of Christ, about to ensue immediately after the "judgment" on Antichrist, announced as imminent in <reference osisRef="Rev.14.7">Re 14:7</reference>. As the former angel "flying through the midst of heaven" (<reference osisRef="Rev.8.13">Re 8:13</reference>) announced "woe," so this angel "flying in the midst of heaven" announced joy. The three angels making this last proclamation of the Gospel, the fall of Babylon (<reference osisRef="Rev.14.8">Re 14:8</reference>), the harlot, and the judgment on the beast worshippers (<reference osisRef="Rev.14.9-Rev.14.11">Re 14:9-11</reference>), the voice from heaven respecting the blessed dead (<reference osisRef="Rev.14.13">Re 14:13</reference>), the vision of the Son of man on the cloud (<reference osisRef="Rev.14.11">Re 14:11</reference>), the harvest (<reference osisRef="Rev.14.15">Re 14:15</reference>), and the vintage (<reference osisRef="Rev.14.18">Re 14:18</reference>), form the compendious summary, amplified in detail in the rest of the book. <div eID="gen42047" type="x-p"/>
entries.eb4b0c6b0e96a14087c97fc3b3b3add42c5da691: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv19273"/><div sID="gen42048" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv19273"/><hi type="bold">7. Fear God--</hi>the forerunner to embracing the love of God manifested in the Gospel. Repentance accompanies faith.<div eID="gen42048" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42049" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">give glory to him--</hi>and not to the beast (compare <reference osisRef="Rev.13.4">Re 13:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.13.16">Jr 13:16</reference>).<div eID="gen42049" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42050" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the hour of his judgment--</hi>"The hour" implies the definite time. "Judgment," not the general judgment, but that up on Babylon, the beast, and his worshippers (<reference osisRef="Rev.14.8-Rev.14.12">Re 14:8-12</reference>).<div eID="gen42050" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42051" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">worship him that made heaven--</hi>not Antichrist (compare <reference osisRef="Acts.14.15">Ac 14:15</reference>).<div eID="gen42051" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42052" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">sea ... fountains--</hi>distinguished also in <reference osisRef="Rev.8.8">Re 8:8</reference>, <reference osisRef="Rev.8.10">10</reference>. <div eID="gen42052" type="x-p"/>
entries.b64a9827ace129c97b634690ee826c5a2ddb9b14: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv19274"/><div sID="gen42053" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv19274"/><hi type="bold">8. another--</hi>So Vulgate. But A, B, Syriac, and Andreas add, "a second"; "another, a second angel."<div eID="gen42053" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42054" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Babylon--</hi>here first mentioned; identical with the harlot, the apostate Church; distinct from the beast, and judged separately.<div eID="gen42054" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42055" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">is fallen--</hi>anticipation of <reference osisRef="Rev.18.2">Re 18:2</reference>. A, Vulgate, Syriac, and Andreas support the second "is fallen." But B, C, and Coptic omit it.<div eID="gen42055" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42056" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">that great city--</hi>A, B, C, Vulgate, Syriac, and Coptic omit "city." Then translate, "Babylon the great." The ulterior and exhaustive fulfilment of <reference osisRef="Isa.21.9">Is 21:9</reference>.<div eID="gen42056" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42057" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">because--</hi>So Andreas. But A, C, Vulgate, and Syriac read, "which." B and Coptic omit it. Even reading "which," we must understand it as giving the reason of her fall.<div eID="gen42057" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42058" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">all nations--</hi>A, B and C read, "all the nations."<div eID="gen42058" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42059" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the wine of the wrath of her fornication--</hi>the wine of the wrath of God, the consequence of her fornication. As she made the nations drunk with the wine of her fornication, so she herself shall be made drunk with the wine of God's wrath. <div eID="gen42059" type="x-p"/>
entries.c24a7e2b3adf02cae9da347cf8d0650e99714ed4: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv19275"/><div sID="gen42060" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv19275"/>9. A, B, C, and Andreas read, "another, a third angel." Compare with this verse <reference osisRef="Rev.13.15">Re 13:15</reference>, <reference osisRef="Rev.13.16">16</reference>. <div eID="gen42060" type="x-p"/>
entries.6e496167d27767014187cb5fa777fb4cb7525334: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv19276"/><div sID="gen42061" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv19276"/><hi type="bold">10. The same--</hi>Greek, "he also," as the just and inevitable retribution.<div eID="gen42061" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42062" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">wine of ... wrath of God--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Ps.75.8">Psa 75:8</reference>).<div eID="gen42062" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42063" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">without mixture--</hi>whereas wine was so commonly mixed with water that to mix wine is used in Greek for to pour out wine; this wine of God's wrath is undiluted; there is no drop of water to cool its heat. Naught of grace or hope is blended with it. This terrible threat may well raise us above the fear of man's threats. This unmixed cup is already mingled and prepared for Satan and the beast's followers.<div eID="gen42063" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42064" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">indignation--</hi>Greek, "orges," "abiding wrath," But the Greek for "wrath" above (Greek, "thumou") is boiling indignation, from (Greek, "thuo") a root meaning "to boil"; this is temporary ebullition of anger; that is lasting [Ammonius], and accompanied with a purpose of vengeance [Origen on Psalm 2:5].<div eID="gen42064" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42065" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">tormented ... in the presence of ... angels--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Ps.49.14">Psa 49:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.58.10">58:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.139.21">139:21</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.66.24">Is 66:24</reference>). God's enemies are regarded by the saints as their enemies, and when the day of probation is past, their mind shall be so entirely one with God's, that they shall rejoice in witnessing visibly the judicial vindication of God's righteousness in sinners' punishment. <div eID="gen42065" type="x-p"/>
entries.f7191b050becafc059b492a624074a2a077caac7: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv19277"/><div sID="gen42066" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv19277"/><hi type="bold">11. for ever and ever--</hi>Greek, "unto ages of ages."<div eID="gen42066" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42067" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">no rest day nor night--</hi>Contrast the very different sense in which the same is said of the four living creatures in heaven, "They rest not day and night, saying, Holy, holy, holy"; yet they do "rest" in another sense; they rest from sin and sorrow, weariness and weakness, trial and temptation (<reference osisRef="Rev.14.13">Re 14:13</reference>); the lost have no rest from sin and Satan, terror, torment, and remorse. <div eID="gen42067" type="x-p"/>
entries.1ab79a8094bc08567f5d63850b17d612449b09ec: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv19278"/><div sID="gen42068" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv19278"/><hi type="bold">12. Here, &c.--</hi>resumed from <reference osisRef="Rev.13.10">Re 13:10</reference>; see on <reference osisRef="Rev.13.10">Re 13:10</reference>. In the fiery ordeal of persecution which awaits all who will not worship the beast, the faith and patience of the followers of God and Jesus shall be put to the test, and proved.<div eID="gen42068" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42069" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">patience--</hi>Greek, "hupomene," "patient, persevering endurance." The second "here" is omitted in A, B, C, Vulgate, Syriac, Coptic, and Primasius. Translate, "Here is the endurance of the saints, who keep," &c.<div eID="gen42069" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42070" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the faith of Jesus--</hi>the faith which has Jesus for its object. <div eID="gen42070" type="x-p"/>
entries.ca9a3edf1401d37ad2dad6910aa30126e71f7ac9: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv19279"/><div sID="gen42071" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv19279"/>13. Encouragement to cheer those persecuted under the beast.<div eID="gen42071" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42072" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Write--</hi>to put it on record for ever.<div eID="gen42072" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42073" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Blessed--</hi>in resting from their toils, and, in the case of the saints just before alluded to as persecuted by the beast, in resting from persecutions. Their full blessedness is now "from henceforth," that is, FROM THIS TIME, when the judgment on the beast and the harvest gatherings of the elect are imminent. The time so earnestly longed for by former martyrs is now all but come; the full number of their fellow servants is on the verge of completion; they have no longer to "rest (the same Greek as here, anapausis) yet for a little season," their eternal rest, or cessation from toils (<reference osisRef="2Thess.1.7">2Th 1:7</reference>; Greek, "anesis," relaxation after hardships. <reference osisRef="Heb.4.9">He 4:9</reference>, <reference osisRef="Heb.4.10">10</reference>, sabbatism of rest; and Greek, "catapausis," akin to the Greek here) is close at hand now. They are blessed in being about to sit down to the marriage supper of the Lamb (<reference osisRef="Rev.19.9">Re 19:9</reference>), and in having part in the first resurrection (<reference osisRef="Rev.20.6">Re 20:6</reference>), and in having right to the tree of life (<reference osisRef="Rev.22.14">Re 22:14</reference>). In <reference osisRef="Rev.14.14-Rev.14.16">Re 14:14-16</reference> follows the explanation of why they are pronounced "blessed" now in particular, namely, the Son of man on the cloud is just coming to gather them in as the harvest ripe for garner.<div eID="gen42073" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42074" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Yea, saith the Spirit--</hi>The words of God the Father (the "voice from heaven") are echoed back and confirmed by the Spirit (speaking in the Word, <reference osisRef="Rev.2.7">Re 2:7</reference>; 22:17; and in the saints, <reference osisRef="2Cor.5.5">2Co 5:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Pet.4.14">1Pe 4:14</reference>). All "God's promises in Christ are yea" (<reference osisRef="2Cor.1.20">2Co 1:20</reference>).<div eID="gen42074" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42075" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">unto me--</hi>omitted in A, B, C, Vulgate, Syriac, and Coptic.<div eID="gen42075" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42076" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">that they may--</hi>The Greek includes also the idea, They are blessed, in that they SHALL rest from their toils (so the Greek).<div eID="gen42076" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42077" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">and--</hi>So B and Andreas read. But A, C, Vulgate, and Syriac read "for." They rest from their toils because their time for toil is past; they enter on the blessed rest because of their faith evinced by their works which, therefore, "follow WITH (so the Greek) them." Their works are specified because respect is had to the coming judgment, wherein every man shall be "judged according to his works." His works do not go before the believer, nor even go by his side, but follow him at the same time that they go with him as a proof that he is Christ's. <div eID="gen42077" type="x-p"/>
entries.910d8651732c1a36d3db51768f7f3f1b018cf67a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv19280"/><div sID="gen42078" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv19280"/><hi type="bold">14. crown--</hi>Greek, "stephanon," "garland" of victory; not His diadem as a king. The victory is described in detail, <reference osisRef="Rev.19.11-Rev.19.21">Re 19:11-21</reference>.<div eID="gen42078" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42079" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">one sat--</hi>"one sitting," Greek, "cathemenon homoion," is the reading of A, B, C, Vulgate, and Coptic. <div eID="gen42079" type="x-p"/>
entries.e2944521dec9396c9e73a58fb02710f86abdede0: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv19281"/><div sID="gen42080" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv19281"/><hi type="bold">15. Thrust in--</hi>Greek, "Send." The angel does not command the "Son of man" (<reference osisRef="Rev.14.14">Re 14:14</reference>), but is the mere messenger announcing to the Son the will of God the Father, in whose hands are kept the times and the seasons.<div eID="gen42080" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42081" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">thy sickle--</hi>alluding to <reference osisRef="Mark.4.29">Mr 4:29</reference>, where also it is "sendeth the sickle." The Son sends His sickle-bearing angel to reap the righteous when fully ripe.<div eID="gen42081" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42082" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">harvest--</hi>the harvest crop. By the harvest-reaping the elect righteous are gathered out; by the vintage the Antichristian offenders are removed out of the earth, the scene of Christ's coming kingdom. The Son of man Himself, with a golden crown, is introduced in the harvest-gathering of the elect, a mere angel in the vintage (<reference osisRef="Rev.14.18-Rev.14.20">Re 14:18-20</reference>).<div eID="gen42082" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42083" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">is ripe--</hi>literally, "is dried." Ripe for glory. <div eID="gen42083" type="x-p"/>
entries.a95515da226b0800b6dc912c2982d53285541d7a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv19282"/><div sID="gen42084" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv19282"/><hi type="bold">16. thrust in--</hi>Greek, "cast." <div eID="gen42084" type="x-p"/>
entries.ab16fbb918e6a58132be0e01111bc5c97e502b0d: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv19283"/><div sID="gen42085" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv19283"/><hi type="bold">17. out of the temple ... in heaven--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Rev.11.19">Re 11:19</reference>). <div eID="gen42085" type="x-p"/>
entries.1f7cd91f098ad73e9e16b7697540a093a25fda6f: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv19284"/><div sID="gen42086" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv19284"/><hi type="bold">18. from the altar--</hi>upon which were offered the incense-accompanied prayers of all saints, which bring down in answer God's fiery judgment on the Church's foes, the fire being taken from the altar and cast upon the earth.<div eID="gen42086" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42087" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">fully ripe--</hi>Greek, "come to their acme"; ripe for punishment. <div eID="gen42087" type="x-p"/>
entries.7e3f65731c8eeccdec42dd24f2f729688f9d49eb: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv19285"/><div sID="gen42088" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv19285"/>19. "The vine" is what is the subject of judgment because its grapes are not what God looked for considering its careful culture, but "wild grapes" (<reference osisRef="Isa.5.1-Isa.5.30">Is 5:1-30</reference>). The apostate world of Christendom, not the world of heathendom who have not heard of Christ, is the object of judgment. Compare the emblem, <reference osisRef="Rev.19.15">Re 19:15</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.63.2">Is 63:2</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.63.3">3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Joel.3.13">Joe 3:13</reference>. <div eID="gen42088" type="x-p"/>
entries.e45e73f6c5abc63c323e2516a030c33e4bf35ec3: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv19286"/><div sID="gen42089" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv19286"/><hi type="bold">20. without the city--</hi>Jerusalem. The scene of the blood-shedding of Christ and His people shall be also the scene of God's vengeance on the Antichristian foe. Compare the "horsemen," <reference osisRef="Rev.9.16">Re 9:16</reference>, <reference osisRef="Rev.9.17">17</reference>.<div eID="gen42089" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42090" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">blood--</hi>answering to the red wine. The slaughter of the apostates is what is here spoken of, not their eternal punishment.<div eID="gen42090" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42091" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">even unto the horse bridles--</hi>of the avenging "armies of heaven."<div eID="gen42091" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42092" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">by the space of a thousand ... six hundred furlongs--</hi>literally, "a thousand six hundred furlongs off" [W. Kelly]. Sixteen hundred is a square number; four by four by one hundred. The four quarters, north, south, east, and west, of the Holy Land, or else of the world (the completeness and universality of the world-wide destruction being hereby indicated). It does not exactly answer to the length of Palestine as given by Jerome, one hundred sixty Roman miles. Bengel thinks the valley of Kedron, between Jerusalem and the Mount of Olives, is meant, the torrent in that valley being about to be discolored with blood to the extent of sixteen hundred furlongs. This view accords with Joel's prophecy that the valley of Jehoshaphat is to be the scene of the overthrow of the Antichristian foes. <chapter eID="Rev.14"/>

entries.1beb07cf0c56d209cc8535100eb6907669b4ab68: <div eID="gen56413" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen56414" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen56415" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen56415" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen56414" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen56416" type="x-p"/> The Lamb on mount Sion, and his company and their character, <reference osisRef="Rev.14.1-Rev.14.5">Rev 14:1-5</reference>. The angel flying in the midst of heaven, with the everlasting Gospel, <reference osisRef="Rev.14.6">Rev 14:6</reference>, <reference osisRef="Rev.14.7">Rev 14:7</reference>. Another angel proclaims the fall of Babylon, <reference osisRef="Rev.14.8">Rev 14:8</reference>. A third angel denounces God's judgments against those who worship the beast or his image, <reference osisRef="Rev.14.9-Rev.14.11">Rev 14:9-11</reference>. The patience of the saints, and the blessedness of them who die in the Lord, <reference osisRef="Rev.14.12">Rev 14:12</reference>, <reference osisRef="Rev.14.13">Rev 14:13</reference>. The man on the white cloud, with a sickle, reaping the earth, <reference osisRef="Rev.14.14-Rev.14.16">Rev 14:14-16</reference>. The angel with the sickle commanded by another angel, who had power over fire, to gather the clusters of the vines of the earth, <reference osisRef="Rev.14.17">Rev 14:17</reference>, <reference osisRef="Rev.14.18">Rev 14:18</reference>. They are gathered and thrown into the great winepress of God's wrath, which is trodden without the city, and the blood comes out 1600 furlongs, <reference osisRef="Rev.14.19">Rev 14:19</reference>, <reference osisRef="Rev.14.20">Rev 14:20</reference>. <div eID="gen56416" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen56417" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen56417" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen56418" type="x-p"/> A Lamb stood on the mount Sion - This represents Jesus Christ in his sacrificial office; mount Sion was a type of the Christian Church. <div eID="gen56418" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen56419" type="x-p"/> And with him a hundred forty and four thousand - Representing those who were converted to Christianity from among the Jews. See <reference osisRef="Rev.7.4">Rev 7:4</reference>. <div eID="gen56419" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen56420" type="x-p"/> His Father's name written in their foreheads - They were professedly, openly, and practically, the children of God, by faith in Christ Jesus. Different sects of idolaters have the peculiar mark of their god on their foreheads. This is practised in the east to the present day, and the mark is called the sectarial mark. Between eighty and ninety different figures are found on the foreheads of different Hindoo deities and their followers. <div eID="gen56420" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen56421" type="x-p"/> Almost every MS. of importance, as well as most of the versions and many of the fathers, read this clause thus: Having His Name and his Father's name written upon their foreheads. This is undoubtedly the true reading, and is properly received by Griesbach into the text.
entries.1c1a80e21b0f9955260133abf83fc6e65afc3b51: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen56421" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen56422" type="x-p"/> The voice of many waters - That is, of multitudes of various nations. <div eID="gen56422" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen56423" type="x-p"/> The voice of harpers - Though the sounds were many and apparently confused, yet both harmony and melody were preserved.
entries.7d47d3049b1c6839dcbafa1d17916e3ae17379dd: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen56423" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen56424" type="x-p"/> They sung - a new song - See on <reference osisRef="Rev.5.9">Rev 5:9</reference> (note). <div eID="gen56424" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen56425" type="x-p"/> No man could learn that song - As none but genuine Christians can worship God acceptably, because they approach him through the only Mediator, so none can understand the deep things of God but such; nor can others know the cause why true believers exult so much in God through Christ, because they know not the communion which such hold with the Father and the Son through the Holy Ghost.
entries.1ddf9550f24f80cc560212aa015bb5d4e95f5278: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen56425" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen56426" type="x-p"/> These are they which were not defiled with women - They are pure from idolatry, and are presented as unspotted virgins to their Lord and Savior Christ. See <reference osisRef="2Cor.11.2">2Cor 11:2</reference>. There may be an allusion here to the Israelites committing idolatry, through the means of their criminal connection with the Midianitish women. See <reference osisRef="Num.25.1-Num.25.4">Num 25:1-4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Num.31.16">Num 31:16</reference>. <div eID="gen56426" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen56427" type="x-p"/> Follow the Lamb whithersoever he goeth - They go through good and through evil report, bear his reproach, and love not their lives even to the death. <div eID="gen56427" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen56428" type="x-p"/> The first fruits unto God - The reference appears to be to those Jews who were the first converts to Christianity.
entries.d2a7b92d0309574a70bb227d7f7346682bdeb30b: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen56428" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen56429" type="x-p"/> In their mouth was found no guile - When brought before kings and rulers they did not dissemble, but boldly confessed the Lord Jesus.
entries.18d2158f546f7bd13a1ea470cc3c34484ed17bd6: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen56429" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen56430" type="x-p"/> Another angel fly in the midst of heaven, having the everlasting Gospel - Whether this angel mean any more than a particular dispensation of providence and grace, by which the Gospel shall be rapidly sent throughout the whole world; or whether it mean any especial messenger, order of preachers, people, or society of Christians, whose professed object it is to send the Gospel of the kingdom throughout the earth, we know not. But the vision seems truly descriptive of a late institution, entitled The British and Foreign Bible Society, whose object it is to print and circulate the Scriptures of the Old and New Testaments, through all the habitable world, and in all the languages spoken on the face of the earth. Already they have been the instruments, by actually printing (or by affording the means to different nations to print for themselves) the Bible in a vast number of languages and dialects, so that it has been sent in hundreds of thousands of copies, in whole or in part, to almost every part of the globe: viz., in their native language to the Welsh; in Erse to the Irish; in Gaelic to the Highlands of Scotland; in Manks to the Isle of Man; in French, Italian, Portuguese, and Spanish, to those countries and Switzerland; in Low Dutch to Holland, etc.; in High Dutch to Germany, Prussia, etc. Through them a similar society has been established at St. Petersburgh, by which the Bible has been sent in Slavonic to the Russians; and in different dialects to the people of that vast empire; besides the Turkish, Tartaric, and Calmuck. They have also sent the Holy Scriptures in ancient and modern Greek to Asia Minor and the different isles of the Mediterranean Sea; in Arabic and Ethiopic to Egypt and Abyssinia; in Syriac to the Holy Land, and to the Christians at Travancore. They have also greatly and effectually assisted a very worthy society in the East Indies, whose indefatigable and incomparable missionaries, the Rev. Messrs. Carey, Marshman, and Ward, have translated the Scriptures into the principal languages of India; and they have furnished the means of printing a complete translation of the New Testament in the Chinese language at Canton, by the Rev. Mr. Morrison. In short, almost every nation in the universe has, through this society, directly or indirectly received, or is receiving, the words of eternal life; so that it appears to answer the description of the Apocalyptic "angel, flying in the midst of heaven, having the everlasting Gospel to preach unto them that dwell on the earth, and to every nation, and kindred, and tongue, and people."
entries.6df37c2f4a9b1311d99ff307bedc754ca6683d0d: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen56430" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen56431" type="x-p"/> Fear God, and give glory to him - This is the general language of the sacred writings. Worship the true God, the creator and governor of all things; and give him glory, for to him alone, not to idols or men, all glory and honor belong.
entries.24be8a2f943c37940fb5021a6ed87bdf2882e2ca: <hi type="bold">Verse 8</hi> <div eID="gen56431" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen56432" type="x-p"/> Babylon is fallen, is fallen - This is generally understood to be a prediction concerning Rome; and it is certain that Rome, in the rabbinical writings, is termed Babylon. <div eID="gen56432" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen56433" type="x-p"/> That great city - Among the same writers this city is styled קרתא רבתא karta rabbetha, the great city; and רומי רבתא Romi rabbetha, the great Rome. But which Rome is meant? Pagan or Papal Rome? Some parts of the description apply best to the former. <div eID="gen56433" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen56434" type="x-p"/> The wine of the wrath of her fornication - There is an allusion here to a custom of impure women, who give philtres or love potions to those whom they wish to seduce and bind to their will; and these potions are generally of an intoxicating nature, greatly inflaming the blood, and disturbing the intellect. <div eID="gen56434" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen56435" type="x-p"/> Fornication and adultery are frequently used in Scripture as emblems of idolatry and false worship. <div eID="gen56435" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen56436" type="x-p"/> The wine of the wrath is another expression for the envenomed or poisoned cup given by such women. <div eID="gen56436" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen56437" type="x-p"/> No nation of the earth spread their idolatries so far as the ancient Romans; they were as extensive as their conquests. And papal Rome has been not less active in disseminating her superstitions. She has given her rituals, but not the everlasting Gospel, to most nations of the earth.
entries.3ac509ebbda395454d4c0f9aebbccdbd2b238bde: <hi type="bold">Verse 9</hi> <div eID="gen56437" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen56438" type="x-p"/> And the third angel followed - Bishop Bale considers these three angels as three descriptions of preachers, who should bear their testimony against the corruptions of the papal Church. <div eID="gen56438" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen56439" type="x-p"/> The beast and his image - See the notes on Revelation 13:1-18 (note). <div eID="gen56439" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen56440" type="x-p"/> Mark in his forehead - Such as the sectarial marks of the idolatrous Hindoos, as has been observed before.
entries.6596886c1634505339d094e558106e1cd0c95889: <hi type="bold">Verse 10</hi> <div eID="gen56440" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen56441" type="x-p"/> The wine of the wrath of God - As they have drunk the intoxicating wine of idolatry or spiritual fornication, they shall now drink the wine of God's wrath, which is poured out into the cup of his indignation. This is an allusion to the poisoned cup, which certain criminals were obliged to drink, on which ensued speedy death. See on <reference osisRef="Heb.2.9">Heb 2:9</reference> (note). <div eID="gen56441" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen56442" type="x-p"/> Shall be tormented with fire and brimstone - An allusion to the punishment of Sodom and Gomorrha for their unnatural crimes. <div eID="gen56442" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen56443" type="x-p"/> Presence of the holy angels, and - of the Lamb - These being the instruments employed in their destruction; the Lamb - the Lord Jesus Christ, acting as judge.
entries.c8f521d2a78f8e7ec22eed45f363a008dd26a42a: <hi type="bold">Verse 11</hi> <div eID="gen56443" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen56444" type="x-p"/> The smoke of their torment - Still an allusion to the destruction of Sodom and Gomorrha.
entries.3cbb453249ded84dddf05d78416ee2bb7a0468e5: <hi type="bold">Verse 12</hi> <div eID="gen56444" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen56445" type="x-p"/> Here is the patience of the saints - Here the faith of the true Christians shall be proved; they will follow the Lamb whithersoever he goeth, they keep the commandments of God, and are steadfast in the faith of our Lord Jesus Christ. Sometimes ἡ ὑπομονη, patience or perseverance, is taken for the reward of these virtues; the text therefore may be thus understood: Here is the reward of the perseverance of the true Christians; for although they die for the testimony of Jesus, yet they shall be unutterably blessed. See the next verse.
entries.476082b28299237b4c9d64cba9c7c8d66267cfb7: <hi type="bold">Verse 13</hi> <div eID="gen56445" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen56446" type="x-p"/> I heard a voice from heaven - As the information now to be given was of the utmost importance, it is solemnly communicated by a voice from heaven; and the apostle is commanded to write or record what is said. <div eID="gen56446" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen56447" type="x-p"/> Blessed are the dead - Happy are they. They are happy in two respects: <div eID="gen56447" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen56448" type="x-p"/> 1. They do not see the evil that shall come upon the world, and are exempted from any farther sufferings. <div eID="gen56448" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen56449" type="x-p"/> 2. They actually and conscientiously enjoy happiness in a state of blessedness. <div eID="gen56449" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen56450" type="x-p"/> In the first sense, Happy are the dead! is a proverb frequently to be met in the Greek and Roman poets. Ex. gr. Τρις μακαρες Δαναοι και τετρακις, οἱ τοτ' ολοντο Τροιῃ εν ευρειη, χαριν Ατρειδῃσι φεροντες. Ὡς δη εγωγ' οφελον θανεειν και ποτμον επισπειν Ηματι τῳ, ὁτε μοι πλειστοι χαλκηρεα δουρα Τρωες επερῥιψαν περι Πηλειωνι θανοντι. <div eID="gen56450" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen56451" type="x-p"/> Odyss., lib. v. ver. 306. <div eID="gen56451" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen56452" type="x-p"/> Happy, thrice happy; who, in battle slain, <div eID="gen56452" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen56453" type="x-p"/> Press'd, in Atrides' cause, the Trojan plain: <div eID="gen56453" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen56454" type="x-p"/> O, had I died before that well fought wall; <div eID="gen56454" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen56455" type="x-p"/> Had some distinguished day renown'd my fall, <div eID="gen56455" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen56456" type="x-p"/> Such as was that when showers of javelins fled, <div eID="gen56456" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen56457" type="x-p"/> From conquering Troy, around Achilles dead. <div eID="gen56457" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen56458" type="x-p"/> Pope. <div eID="gen56458" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen56459" type="x-p"/> Thus imitated by the prince of the Roman poets: - <div eID="gen56459" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen56460" type="x-p"/> Extemplo Aeneae solvuntur frigore membra. <div eID="gen56460" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen56461" type="x-p"/> Ingemit, et, duplices tendens ad sidera palmas, <div eID="gen56461" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen56462" type="x-p"/> Talia voce refert: O terque quaterque beati, <div eID="gen56462" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen56463" type="x-p"/> Queis ante ora patrum Trojae sub moenibus altis <div eID="gen56463" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen56464" type="x-p"/> Contigit oppetere! O Danaum fortissime gentis <div eID="gen56464" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen56465" type="x-p"/> Tydide, mene Iliacis occumbere campis <div eID="gen56465" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen56466" type="x-p"/> Non potuisse? tuaque animam hanc effundere dextra? <div eID="gen56466" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen56467" type="x-p"/> Saevus ubi Aeacidae telo jacet Hector, ubi ingens <div eID="gen56467" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen56468" type="x-p"/> Sarpedon: ubi tot Simois correpta sub undis <div eID="gen56468" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen56469" type="x-p"/> Scuta virum, galeasque, et fortis corpora volvit. <div eID="gen56469" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen56470" type="x-p"/> Virg., Aen. i., ver. 93. "In horror fix'd the Trojan hero stands, <div eID="gen56470" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen56471" type="x-p"/> He groans, and spreads to heaven his lifted hands. <div eID="gen56471" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen56472" type="x-p"/> Thrice happy those whose fate it was to fall, <div eID="gen56472" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen56473" type="x-p"/> Exclaims the chief, before the Trojan wall! <div eID="gen56473" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen56474" type="x-p"/> O, 'twas a glorious fate to die in fight! <div eID="gen56474" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen56475" type="x-p"/> To die so bravely in their parents' sight! <div eID="gen56475" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen56476" type="x-p"/> O, had I there, beneath Tydides' hand, <div eID="gen56476" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen56477" type="x-p"/> That bravest hero of the Grecian band, <div eID="gen56477" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen56478" type="x-p"/> Pour'd out this soul, with martial glory fired, <div eID="gen56478" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen56479" type="x-p"/> And in the plain triumphantly expired, <div eID="gen56479" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen56480" type="x-p"/> Where Hector fell, by fierce Achilles' spear, <div eID="gen56480" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen56481" type="x-p"/> And great Sarpedon, the renown'd in war; <div eID="gen56481" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen56482" type="x-p"/> Where Simois' stream, encumber'd with the slain, <div eID="gen56482" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen56483" type="x-p"/> Rolls shields and helms and heroes to the main." <div eID="gen56483" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen56484" type="x-p"/> Pitt. <div eID="gen56484" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen56485" type="x-p"/> Which die in the Lord - These are the only glorious dead. They die, not in the field of battle, in either what are called lawful or unlawful wars against their fellow men; but they die in the cause of God, they die under the smile and approbation of God, and they die to live and reign with God for ever and ever. <div eID="gen56485" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen56486" type="x-p"/> From henceforth - Απαρτι· From this time; now; immediately. This word is joined to the following by many MSS. and some versions. It was a maxim among the Jews, that as soon as the souls of the just departed from this life they ascended immediately to heaven. <div eID="gen56486" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen56487" type="x-p"/> Yea, saith the Spirit - The Holy Spirit confirms the declaration from heaven, and assigns the reasons of it. <div eID="gen56487" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen56488" type="x-p"/> That they may rest from their labors - Have no more tribulation and distress. <div eID="gen56488" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen56489" type="x-p"/> And their works do follow there - Εργα αυτων ακολουθει μετ' αυτων· And their works follow With them. They are in company. Here is an elegant prosopopoeia or personification; their good works, sufferings, etc., are represented as so many companions escorting them on their way to the kingdom of God. <div eID="gen56489" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen56490" type="x-p"/> There are some good and pertinent things in the Jewish writers on this subject. "Rabbi Jonathan taught, If a man perform one righteous action in this life, it goes before him into the world to come. But if a man commit one crime, it cleaves to him, and drags him to the day of judgment." Sota, fol. 3, 2. Avoda Sara, fol. 5, 1. "Come and see, If any man observe a precept, that work ascends to God, and says, Such a one performed me. But if a man transgress the law, that sin ascends to the holy blessed God, and says, I came from such a one, who has performed me." Sohar Levit., fol. 34, col. 136. Here the same personification is observed as that in the text. "In that hour in which a man passes from this life into eternity, all his works precede him; and there they say unto him, 'This and that thou hast done in such a place on such a day.' This he shall acknowledge. They shall require that he shall subscribe this with his own hand, as it is written, <reference osisRef="Job.37.7">Job 37:7</reference>; each man shall subscribe with his own hand; and not only this, but he shall acknowledge that the sentence brought against him is most just." Taanith, fol. 11, 1. <div eID="gen56490" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen56491" type="x-p"/> The following elegant similitude Schoettgen gives from Sepher Hachayim, Part II., fol. 47, 1, 2. "A certain man had three friends, two of whom he loved; but the third he did not highly esteem. On a time the king commanded him to be called before him; and being alarmed, he sought to find an advocate. He went to that friend whom he loved most, but he utterly refused to go with him. The second offered to go with him as far as the door of the king's palace, but refused to speak a word in his behalf. The third, whom he loved least, not only went with him, but pleaded his cause so well before the king that he was cleared from all blame. In like manner, every man has three friends, when he is cited by death to appear before God. The first friend, whom he loved most, viz., his money, cannot accompany him at all. His second, viz., his relations and neighbors, accompanied him only to the grave, and then returned; but could not deliver him from the Judge. The third friend, whom he held but in little esteem, viz., the law and his good works, went with him to the king, and delivered him from judgment." The meaning of this most plainly is, that nothing except the deeds of good and evil men shall accompany them to the judgment-seat of God, and that a man's lot will be in the other world as his conduct has been in this; Their works follow with them.
entries.d281da614e33a8d4dd8cbd06169923fc91574b7c: <hi type="bold">Verse 14</hi> <div eID="gen56491" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen56492" type="x-p"/> A white cloud - It is supposed that, from this verse to the end of the chapter, the destruction of Rome is represented under the symbols of harvest and vintage; images very frequent among the ancient prophets, by which they represented the destruction and excision of nations. See <reference osisRef="Joe.3.12-Joe.3.14">Joe 3:12-14</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.17.5">Isa 17:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.63.1">Isa 63:1</reference>; and <reference osisRef="Mat.13.37">Mat 13:37</reference>. <div eID="gen56492" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen56493" type="x-p"/> A golden crown - In token of victory and regal power.
entries.88e4e732141265418d362cbca5a2c27cf44d37d0: <hi type="bold">Verse 15</hi> <div eID="gen56493" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen56494" type="x-p"/> Thrust in thy sickle - Execute the judgments which God has decreed. <div eID="gen56494" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen56495" type="x-p"/> For the harvest of the earth is ripe - The cup of the people's iniquity is full.
entries.67f30d3193cbf4ba29ec6d7d21f46a8874c189ce: <hi type="bold">Verse 16</hi> <div eID="gen56495" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen56496" type="x-p"/> The earth was reaped - The judgments were executed. But where, or on whom, who can tell?
entries.102f5e419d1fd2e27a4584db3740fd24fd3b03a4: <hi type="bold">Verse 18</hi> <div eID="gen56496" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen56497" type="x-p"/> Power over fire - Probably meaning the same angel which is mentioned, <reference osisRef="Rev.8.3">Rev 8:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.9.13">Rev 9:13</reference>, who stood by the altar of burnt-offering, having authority over its fire to offer that incense to God which represents the prayers of the saints.
entries.5f1a7ffd893d15d2965f0a84bd6609aef5233dc8: <hi type="bold">Verse 19</hi> <div eID="gen56497" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen56498" type="x-p"/> The great winepress of the wrath of God - The place or kingdom where God executes his judgments on the workers of iniquity, whether pagans or persecuting Christians; Rome pagan, or Rome papal.
entries.4a7705828fb806326d28e5f1b56fec3ef8054ac6: <hi type="bold">Verse 20</hi> <div eID="gen56498" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen56499" type="x-p"/> Even unto the horse bridles - A hyperbolical expression, to denote a great effusion of blood. The Jews said, "When Hadrian besieged the city called Bitter, he slew so many that the horses waded in blood up to their mouths." The same kind of hyperbole with that above. See Wetstein on this verse. <div eID="gen56499" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen56500" type="x-p"/> The space of a thousand and six hundred furlongs - It is said that the state of the Church, or St. Peter's patrimony, extends from Rome to the Po, two hundred Italian miles, which make exactly one thousand six hundred furlongs! If this be really so, the coincidence is certainly surprising, and worthy of deep regard. <div eID="gen56500" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen56501" type="x-p"/> On these two last verses pious Quesnel thus speaks: "As the favorable sickle of Jesus Christ reaps his wheat when ripe for heaven, so that of the executioners of his justice cuts off from this life the tares which are only fit for the fire of hell. Then shall the blood of Christ cease to be trampled on by sinners; and that of the wicked shall be eternally trodden down in hell, which is the winepress of the wrath of God. "And the winepress was trodden without the city, eternally without the city of the heavenly Jerusalem, and far from the presence of God; eternally crushed and trodden down by his justice; eternally tormented in body and soul, without any hope either of living or dying! This is the miserable lot and portion of those who shall have despised the law of God, and died in impenitence. My God, pierce my heart with a salutary dread of thy judgments!" <div eID="gen56501" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen56502" type="x-p"/> Whatever these passages may mean, this is a prudent and Christian use of them.  <chapter eID="Rev.14"/> <div eID="gen56502" type="x-p"/>

entries.d30d590a9454fac995af413f4802dab3e2275e24:
CHAPTER XIV ANALYSIS OF THE CHAPTER

IN the previous chapters (12,13) there is a description of the woes and sorrows which, for a long period, would come upon the church, and which would threaten to destroy it. It was proper that this gloomy picture should be relieved, and accordingly this chapter, having much of the aspect of an episode, is thrown in to comfort the hearts of those who should see those troublous times. There were bright scenes beyond, and it was important to direct the eye to them, that the hearts of the sad might be consoled. This chapter, therefore, contains a succession of symbolical representations designed to show the ultimate result of all these things--"to hold out the symbols of ultimate and certain victory."--Prof. Stuart. Those symbols are the following:--

(1.) The vision of the hundred and forty-four thousand on Mount Zion, as emblematic of the final triumph of the redeemed, Re 14:1-5. They have the Father's name in their foreheads, Rev 14:1; they sing a song of victory, Rev 14:2,3; they are found without fault before God's representatives, in this respect, of all that will be saved, Rev 14:4,5.

(2.) The vision of the final triumph of the gospel, Rev 14:6,7. An angel is seen flying in the midst of heaven, having the everlasting gospel to preach to all that dwell upon the earth, and announcing that the end is near: a representation designed to show that the gospel will be thus preached among all nations; and when that is done, the time will draw on when the affairs of the world will be wound up.

(3.) The fall of Babylon, the mighty Antichristian power, Rev 14:8. An angel is seen going forth announcing the glad tidings that this mighty power is overthrown, and that, therefore, its oppressions are come to an end. This, to the church in trouble and persecution, is one of the most comforting of all the assurances that God makes in regard to the future.

(4.) The certain and final destruction of all the upholders of that Antichristian power, Rev 14:9-12. Another angel is seen making proclamation that all the supporters and abettors of this formidable power would drink of the wine of the wrath of God; that they would be tormented with fire and brimstone; and that the smoke of their torment would ascend up for ever and ever.

(5.) The blessedness of all those who die in the Lord; who, amidst the persecutions and trials that were to come upon the church, would be found faithful unto death, Rev 14:13. They would rest from their labours; the works of mercy which they had done on the earth would follow them to the future world, securing rich and eternal blessings there.

(6.) The final overthrow of all the enemies of the church, Rev 14:14-20. This is the grand completion; to this all things are tending; this will be certainly accomplished in due time. This is represented under various emblems:

(a) The Son of man appears seated on a cloud, having on his head a golden crown, and in his hand a sharp sickle--emblem of gathering in the great harvest of the earth, and of his own glorious reign in heaven, Rev 14:14.

(b) An angel is seen coming out of the temple, announcing that the time had come, and calling on the great Reaper to thrust in his sickle, for the harvest of the world was ripe, Rev 14:15.

(c) He that has the sickle thrusts in his sickle to reap the great harvest, Rev 14:16.

(d) Another angel is seen representing the final judgment of God on the wicked, Rev 16:17-20. He also has a sharp sickle; he is commanded by an angel that has power over fire to thrust in his sickle into the earth; he goes forth and gathers the clusters of the vine of the earth, and casts them into the great wine-press of the wrath of God.

This whole chapter, therefore, is designed to relieve the gloom of the former representations. The action of the grand moving panorama is stayed that the mind may not be overwhelmed with gloomy thoughts, but that it may be cheered with the assurance of the final triumph of truth and righteousness.
